opus-5.5.text:
Well, the core problem is the sheer size of the search space. On a 19-by-19 board you have roughly 361 possible moves at the start, and the game can run a couple hundred moves deep, so the number of possible game trajectories is astronomically larger than the number of atoms in the universe. You simply can't brute-force it the way early chess engines more or less could.

But the branching factor alone isn't the whole story. The deeper difficulty is evaluation. In chess you can write a decent heuristic: count material, look at king safety, piece mobility, and you get a reasonable signal about who's winning. In Go, a stone is a stone; there's no obvious material count. Whether a position is good depends on subtle, global things like influence, territory that isn't settled yet, whether a group is alive or dead, and those can hinge on a single move thirty turns later. So even if you could search a few moves ahead, you wouldn't know how to score the leaf positions you arrived at.

That's why the breakthrough with AlphaGo was so interesting to me. It combined two learned intuitions: a policy network that tells you which handful of moves are even worth considering, which collapses that enormous branching factor, and a value network that looks at a board and gives you a gut-feel estimate of who's winning, which replaces the handcrafted evaluation function nobody could write. Then Monte Carlo tree search stitches those together, using a bit of explicit lookahead to correct the errors in the intuition.

So the lesson I take away is that Go is hard not because it requires some exotic kind of reasoning, but because it requires good intuition at scale, the kind of pattern recognition that humans build up over thousands of games. And once you can learn that intuition from data and self-play, the search problem becomes tractable. I think that's a template that generalizes well beyond board games, to robotics and to language models doing reasoning: learn a good prior over actions, learn a good sense of value, and then search a little on top.

r001.rationale: The response says Go positions are hard to evaluate because value depends on subtle, global, often unresolved outcomes. It does not clearly identify the absence of an immediate reward signal for individual moves.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it's actually not that hard anymore, and that's kind of the interesting part. For a long time Go was the poster child for "the thing computers can't do." The branching factor is enormous, something like 250 legal moves per position versus maybe 35 in chess, and the games are long, so brute-force search just falls over. And the other problem was that nobody could write down a good evaluation function. In chess you can at least count material and get something sensible. In Go, whether a group of stones is alive or dead, or whether a shape is "thick" or "thin," is this very holistic, pattern-level judgment that strong human players have but can't really articulate. People used to describe it almost in aesthetic terms.

So the difficulty was never really about computation in the narrow sense. It was that choosing a move requires intuition, and we didn't have a way to put intuition into a program. What changed with AlphaGo was that you could learn that evaluation function from data and from self-play. The policy network basically says "here are the handful of moves a strong player would even consider," which collapses the branching factor, and the value network gives you a sense of who's winning without having to play the game out. Then Monte Carlo tree search just stitches those intuitions together into something that looks like deliberate reasoning.

The reason I still find it instructive is that it's a clean example of the general problem I care about in robotics. The hard part isn't the combinatorics, it's the prior. If you have a good prior over what's worth trying, search becomes tractable. If you don't, no amount of compute saves you. Go is a very pure version of that lesson, with none of the messiness of the physical world, which is exactly why it got solved first.

r001.rationale: The response describes the difficulty of writing a useful evaluation function and of judging board patterns, but does not identify the absence of an immediate reward signal for individual moves.

astra-6.text:
Well, Go is a nice example of a problem where it’s much easier to evaluate an outcome than to figure out the action that gets you there. At the end of the game, you can tell who won. But in the middle of the game, you might have hundreds of legal moves, and whether a particular move is good depends on how both players respond many turns into the future.

You can’t just enumerate all those possibilities—the tree gets too big. And a move can look locally bad, like sacrificing some stones, but put you in a much stronger position later. So you need some way of recognizing promising moves and estimating the long-term value of a position without playing out every possible continuation. That’s the hard part.

r001.rationale: The response says outcomes are easy to evaluate only at the end of the game, while a move’s value depends on how play unfolds many turns later. This communicates that individual moves lack an immediate reward signal.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the rules of Go are very simple, but the space of possible games is enormous. On a typical turn, you might have a couple hundred legal moves, and each one branches into hundreds of responses. So you can’t just search through all the possibilities.

The other difficulty is that it’s hard to tell how good a position is. In chess, counting material gives you a useful starting point. In Go, a stone’s value depends on its relationship to everything else on the board. A move might sacrifice territory locally but build influence that pays off much later.

So choosing a good move requires both an intuition about which possibilities are worth exploring and an ability to evaluate where those possibilities lead. You have to compress this enormous search space into something tractable.

r001.rationale: The response says a move’s value can depend on later outcomes and be hard to evaluate, but it does not identify the absence of an immediate reward signal for individual moves.
